name: Sara Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Millbrook, which is outdoor pigs, about four hundred sows in arks across the fields, plus potatoes and some wheat in the rotation. My main job is the farrowing paddocks, so checking new litters, counting piglets, making sure the sows haven't lain on any. Then feeding, water troughs, fixing electric fence the pigs have rooted under. Mud, mostly. I'm getting better, but I still miss a weak piglet that Jo, the head stockperson, would spot in a second.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to pig farming?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a receptionist at a vet practice for years and I always wanted to be out the back with the animals. When Pablo started school I thought, now or never. That was four years ago. My husband Luis is an electrician, self-employed, and we've got Marta, who's fourteen, and Pablo, nine. I'm the one in our house with the budget spreadsheet; Luis just asks me if we can afford things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then, and probably a bit of 'I told you not to believe everything you read'. I'd say it in the tearoom to Jo, not online. I don't post much, maybe photos of piglets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine, I'd keep learning the job. I use the chatbot now and then, for checking feed amounts or writing a polite email to the school, and that's useful enough. I don't need it to be a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd do the pig welfare course Millbrook's offered me in March, and keep putting two hundred a month into the savings account. Maybe use the AI a bit more for the boring paperwork, the movement records, if Jo lets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It'd feel like a normal year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest risk to your job, if not AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Feed prices, and disease. If swine fever came anywhere near us, the whole farm could be shut. Honestly, a virus in a pig scares me more than a computer does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if a useful bit of AI did turn up, say for the records?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd say fine, and use it. I'm not against things that work. I just want to see them work on someone else's farm first.

S0.say: She'd say 'well, that's that then' and remind people not to believe everything they read. She'd say it in the tearoom, not online.
S0.think: She'd keep learning the job and keep using a chatbot now and then for feed amounts and emails. She doesn't need a revolution.
S0.do: Carries on as normal, taking the pig welfare course in March and saving two hundred a month. Uses AI a bit more for movement records if her boss allows it.
S0.quote: Honestly, a virus in a pig scares me more than a computer does.
S0.fieldNote: Sara is practical and measured: she worries more about disease and feed prices than computers. She's an occasional AI user who wants proof on someone else's farm first. As the household budgeter she thinks in monthly sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, like it always is, and we should be sensible about it. Not panic, not pretend it isn't happening. I'd probably say that to the other mums at football too, because some of them get very worked up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Millbrook would bring in cameras that count piglets and spot a sow lying on one, I'm sure. That's my main job. So I think it'd squeeze my role down to the mud bits, the fencing and the troughs, which aren't the bits I came for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Jo to put me on any training for the new kit, so I'm the one reading the screens. I'd use the chatbot more, maybe ask it to explain things the vet says. And I'd push our savings from three months towards five, which means no new kitchen this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit flat, really, because I came to do the animals and they'd be giving the best bit to a camera.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean at home, with Luis being an electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis is busy. Every farm round here wants new wiring for sensors and chargers. Funny thing is, the same robots that squeeze my job would keep Luis in work for years. So we'd balance out, more or less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that bother you, him doing better out of it than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it's fine, he's earned it. Though I'd remind him who keeps the spreadsheet.

S1.say: She'd say it's change as always and people should be sensible, neither panicking nor pretending. She'd tell the other parents at football the same.
S1.think: She expects cameras to take over counting piglets and spotting crushed ones, squeezing her role down to fencing and troughs.
S1.do: Asks to be trained on the new kit and uses the chatbot to understand what the vet says. Pushes savings from three months towards five by putting off a new kitchen.
S1.feel: Uneasy and a bit flat, since the best part of the job would go to a camera.
S1.quote: Funny thing is, the same robots that squeeze my job would keep Luis in work for years.
S1.fieldNote: Sara's household has a built-in hedge: her husband's electrical work would grow as farms automate. She feels the loss of the part of the job she loves more than a threat to income. Calm, sensible and a little wry about who keeps the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now to the faster ones. The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's scary, but let's keep our heads. The government needs to do something fast, and I'd hope they'd be sensible, not throw money everywhere. I'd say that, but quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's gone, probably in the first year. Luis would have work for a while wiring it all in, maybe two or three years, until the robots can wire themselves. So we've got a bridge, but it's a short one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go through the spreadsheet that first weekend and cut everything that isn't needed: the kitchen fund goes into savings, the second car goes, no holiday. I'd ask Luis if I could work with him as a mate, carrying and pulling cables, because he'd have more jobs than hands. And I'd keep the Millbrook job as long as it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, because Luis would be earning, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marta about her plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta's doing her subject choices next year. She wants to do biology to be a vet nurse. I'd have to sit with her and say, love, I don't know what to tell you to study, and I always know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the mortgage overpayments we've been doing, a hundred a month. Then the kids' clubs, though I'd try to keep one each. Pablo would kick up a fuss about football.

S2.say: She'd say it's scary but people should keep their heads, and hope the government acts fast and sensibly without throwing money everywhere.
S2.think: She thinks her job would go in the first year, while her husband would have wiring work for perhaps two or three years: a bridge, but a short one.
S2.do: Cuts everything non-essential the first weekend, moving the kitchen fund into savings and selling the second car. Asks to work as her husband's electrician's mate while keeping the farm job as long as it lasts, and stops mortgage overpayments.
S2.feel: Anxious but not panicking, because her husband would still be earning.
S2.quote: I'd have to sit with her and say, love, I don't know what to tell you to study, and I always know.
S2.fieldNote: Her husband's trade gives the family a short bridge, which keeps Sara anxious rather than alarmed even with two years. Her sharpest pain is not knowing what to tell her daughter, as the person who 'always knows'. She switches straight into budget mode.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan, so plan. I'd tell people at Millbrook to look at what's growing round here, not what's shrinking. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I think I'd do alright if I start now. Luis would be busy for most of it, and I could learn the trade alongside him. I'd be forty-eight and an apprentice, which is funny, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd sign up for the evening electrical installation course at the college, two nights a week, and work Saturdays with Luis. We'd keep saving, aiming for six months. And I'd talk to Marta about choosing subjects with people at the centre, like nursing rather than lab work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd have a plan, and I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've talked about pigs as the job you always wanted. What would you tell people at Millbrook if you left?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth, more or less. Pigs were my dream. But dreams don't pay the mortgage, and Luis's van does, so I'd get in the van. I'd still miss the piglets though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if, five years on, the robots are doing electrical work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the robots got there before me. But I'd still have earned for a few years, saved, learned something. That's not nothing.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough to plan, so plan, and tell workmates to look at what's growing locally rather than shrinking.
S3.think: She thinks she'd do alright if she starts now, learning her husband's trade while he's busy. Being a 48-year-old apprentice is funny but fine.
S3.do: Signs up for an evening electrical installation course two nights a week and works Saturdays with her husband. Aims for six months of savings and talks to her daughter about choosing people-centred subjects like nursing.
S3.feel: Uneasy but settled by having a plan.
S3.quote: Pigs were my dream. But dreams don't pay the mortgage, and Luis's van does, so I'd get in the van.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Sara a clean plan, retraining into her husband's trade, but it costs her the work she dreamed of. She's honest that the plan only buys time if robots later do electrical work too. Her calm comes from planning, not from feeling safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so let's use it properly. Things like more apprenticeships, not just big speeches. I'd keep saying it in the tearoom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd be fifty-three, Pablo nearly through school, and the mortgage almost done. I think that's alright, honestly. I'd have time to stay with the pigs a while and then move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Millbrook for the first few years, because I'd still be learning, and do the electrical course slowly, one night a week. Around year five I'd go and work with Luis properly. Meanwhile we'd keep overpaying the mortgage so it's done before the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Ten years is two of my five-year spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're waiting a few years before moving. Is that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit. If the end comes in ten years anyway, I'd rather spend some of them doing what I love, mucking out sows in the rain. That's my one bit of romance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Millbrook would you worry about in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo, the head stockperson. She's fifty-eight, and the pigs are her whole life. I'd worry she'd stay till the last day and then not know what to do with herself.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is long, so it should be used properly, with more apprenticeships rather than speeches.
S4.think: At 53, with her son nearly through school and the mortgage almost done, she thinks she'd be alright, with time to stay with the pigs a while and then move.
S4.do: Stays at the pig farm for the first few years while doing the electrical course one night a week, then joins her husband's business around year five. Keeps overpaying the mortgage so it's done before AGI arrives.
S4.feel: Mostly calm; ten years is two of her five-year spreadsheets.
S4.quote: If the end comes in ten years anyway, I'd rather spend some of them doing what I love, mucking out sows in the rain.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Sara allows herself what she called her one bit of romance: staying with the pigs for a while longer. She worries most about her head stockperson, Jo, for whom the work is her whole life. Her plan stays the same as the 5-year one, just slower.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Luis would have work for a bit, but I'd be out straight away and we'd have no time to make a proper plan. What would help is apprenticeships for grown-ups that pay a real wage, so someone like me can learn a trade at forty-three without the family going short.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the animals, honestly. A camera can count piglets, but I'm not sure it'll ever pick one up and warm it in its jacket on a cold night. I'm probably wrong about that, but I'd like to think so.

headlineQuote: A camera can count piglets, but I'm not sure it'll ever pick one up and warm it in its jacket on a cold night.
portrait: Sara Diaz is 43, a junior stockperson in the farrowing paddocks of an outdoor pig and potato farm, four years in after working as a vet receptionist. She's pragmatic, keeps the family budget spreadsheet, and uses AI tools now and then for feed sums and emails. She's calm or uneasy in the milder pictures, sad mainly that cameras might take the part of the job she loves. Her husband's electrical work gives the family a short bridge, so AGI in 2 years makes her anxious rather than alarmed. With 5 or 10 years she'd retrain to work alongside him, taking longer with the pigs if time allows.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd be out of work straight away and the family would have no time to make a proper plan.
whatWouldHelp: Paid adult apprenticeships with a real wage, so someone her age can learn a trade without the family going short.
